title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hook: in the middle of the lament: God's mercies "are new every morning"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lamentations opened with eichah, how, on a city sitting alone, tears on her cheeks. Your line was how she sits alone. Did you keep someone company? Today, a light comes on in the middle of that book. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

Halfway through Lamentations, a man speaks from what feels like the bottom of a pit. He says he's been led into darkness, hedged in so he can't get out, his prayers shut out. Line after line, it gets heavier. Then, with no warning, one sentence changes direction: "This I recall to my mind, Therefore have I hope." Nothing outside him has changed. The city is still in ruins. What changes is what he chooses to remember. Today's word is what he remembers.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE BOTTOM OF A PIT.` → `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` → `NOTHING OUTSIDE HAS CHANGED.`

segments.voice: New every morning. Here's what he recalls, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Surely the LORD's mercies are not consumed, Surely His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; Great is Thy faithfulness." Two words carry the weight. Mercies, in Hebrew chasadim: steady, loyal kindness, the kind that keeps a promise. And compassions, rachamim: tenderness, the way a parent feels toward a child. Those, he says, don't run out. They aren't stored up once, like grain in a barn, to be rationed until they're gone. They arrive fresh. A little like the manna in the wilderness, which came each morning and couldn't be saved for later. Then he adds: "The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; Therefore will I hope in Him." Now notice where all this sits. Not at the end of the book, as a happy ending. Right in the middle. The chapters before it mourn. The chapters after it mourn again. The hope doesn't erase the lament; the lament surrounds it on both sides. It's an honest shape for hope to take: not a door out of sorrow, but a lamp lit inside it. And the claim is small and daily. Not, everything is fine. Just: this morning, something was given that wasn't there last night. The phrase has traveled into the start of the Jewish day. Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul, and ends with these words from Lamentations: rabbah emunatecha, great is your faithfulness. A line from the ruins, said at dawn.
screen: `MERCIES AND COMPASSIONS FAIL NOT.` · `GIVEN FRESH, NOT STORED UP.` · then, large: `HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE LAMENT.` · then: `GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one new mercy today. Go back over the hours since you woke. Find one thing that was given to you today that you didn't earn and didn't plan: light through a window, a kind word, a body that got out of bed, a cup of something warm. Just one. Hold it for a moment, the way the voice in the pit held one memory. If you pray, you can say the old words from the verse: great is thy faithfulness. The bell holds the time.
Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, which thanks God for a new day and ends with Lamentations' words: great is your faithfulness. Today's word.
Your line: a lamp lit inside it. Tonight, name one new mercy from today. Tomorrow when you wake, before you reach for your phone, look for the next one. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

options: call one thing to mind, and hope.

original.note: Hebrew of Lamentations 3:23: new for the mornings.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful line for a coffee mug.

notes: Glosses of chasadim (loyal kindness) and rachamim (parental tenderness) are given without root claims; Keeper please confirm.
The manna comparison is the script's own image, not a claim about the text.
Modeh Ani is paraphrased; its closing 'rabbah emunatecha' echoing Lamentations 3:23 should be confirmed.
Hebrew חֲדָשִׁים לַבְּקָרִים and pronunciation should be checked.
Editor: 'the most honest shape a hope can have' reworded without the superlative; repeated 'Settle, and breathe' practice opener removed.

Auditor (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: the Judaism path quoted the KJV (3:21–24); now JPS 1917, checked against the JPS 1917 text. The wording of 3:22 differs in meaning: KJV 'that we are not consumed', JPS 'Surely the LORD's mercies are not consumed' (the Hebrew tamnu is read both ways). The teach's 'those don't run out' now matches the quoted text directly.
